## Introduction & background

Antennas interact heavily with the space around them. The "near-field" region immediately surrounding an antenna contains strong reactive electric and magnetic fields. Introducing a dielectric (like human skin and tissue) or a conductive object (like a metal enclosure) into this near-field violently shifts the capacitance and inductance of the system. This detunes the antenna, ruining the $S_{11}$ match. This is exactly why commercial IoT devices and phones must be perfectly matched *inside* their final plastic casings, rather than in open air.

## Core equations

Near-field boundary approximation:
$$r \approx \frac{2D^2}{\lambda}$$

## What you're building

1. A near-field interference test recording how proximity to a human hand detunes your antenna's resonant frequency.
2. A metal enclosure test tracking the $S_{11}$ shift when an antenna is mounted near or inside a metal chassis.
3. A physical L-match circuit implemented on scrap copper to correct the "installed" mismatch back to a clean 50 Ω.

## Activity

With yesterday's antenna mid-sweep: grab it — record how far the dip moves. Hold it near a metal box, then inside one — record again. If the "installed" match is off, add the [Day 37](https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/day-37.md) L-match on a scrap of copper and capture before/after S11.
